results.title: Synthetic Controls and Weighted Event Studies with Staggered Adoption
results.content: The synthetic control method aims to estimate treatment effects by constructing a weighted combination of control units, which represents what the treated group would have experienced in the absence of receiving the treatment. While DiD estimation assumes that the effects of unobserved confounders are constant over time, the synthetic control method allows for these effects to change over time, by re-weighting the control group so that it has similar pre-intervention characteristics to the treated group. Synthetic Control Methods for Comparative Case Studies: Estimating the Effect of California's Tobacco Control Program. Synthetic control methods are commonly applied in empirical research to estimate the effects of treatments or interventions on aggregate outcomes. The synthetic control method (SCM) is a popular approach for estimating the impact of a treatment on a single unit in panel data settings. In this paper we study estimation of and inference for average treatment effects in a setting with panel data. In this paper we develop new methods for estimating causal effects in settings with panel data, where a subset of units are exposed to a treatment during a subset of periods, and the goal is estimating counterfactual (untreated) outcomes for the treated unit/period combinations. In contrast, if there are few units and many periods, our proposed method approximates a synthetic control estimator where counterfactual outcomes are estimated through a regression of the lagged outcomes for the treated unit on lagged outcomes for the control units. Propensity score methods are widely used for estimating treatment effects from observational studies. A popular approach is to estimate propensity scores by maximum likelihood based on logistic regression, and then apply inverse probability weighted estimators or extensions to estimate treatment effects. The ability of matched sampling and linear regression adjustment to reduce the bias of an estimate of the treatment effect in two sample observational studies is investigated for a simple matching method and five simple estimates. In this paper an extension of this methodology is proposed that allows for estimation of average causal effects with multi-valued treatments while maintaining the advantages of the propensity score approach.

results.title: Multivariate Statistical Inference and Permutation Testing | Nature Research Intelligence
results.content: # Multivariate Statistical Inference and Permutation Testing. * Multivariate Statistical Inference and Permutation Testing. Multivariate statistical inference encompasses methods that evaluate multiple outcomes or parameters jointly, allowing researchers to understand complex interdependencies within data. Permutation testing is a nonparametric approach that recalculates test statistics for many rearrangements of the observed data, thereby constructing an empirical distribution under the null hypothesis without strict reliance on distributional assumptions. Recent studies have illustrated the application of permutation-based methods to power assessments in nonparametric settings. In particular, innovative Monte Carlo approaches have been employed to derive empirical sample size predictions using Kruskal–Wallis tests integrated with Bernstein fits, reflecting a promising synergy between simulation techniques and classical nonparametric inference. These results underscore improved predictive accuracy in scenarios where traditional ANOVA assumptions do not hold, thereby broadening the applicability of permutation methods to complex real-world datasets [4]. Recent developments have focused on refining permutation tests to ensure both finite-sample exactness and asymptotic validity in multivariate settings. Advanced methodologies include robust permutation tests for correlation and regression coefficients, which actively address issues of Type I errors and directional misinterpretations in bivariate and multivariate dependencies [1]. Additionally, extensions to ordinal measures of association have improved the accuracy and interpretation of nonparametric tests in situations where data are inherently rank-based, providing asymptotically valid inference where exact tests often falter [2]. Complementing these efforts, novel permutation procedures for longitudinal data have been proposed to account for dependency structures in repeated measures designs, delivering more reliable error control and enhancing the practical utility of multivariate inference [3]. **Permutation test:** A nonparametric method that involves rearranging labels of the observed data to generate an empirical distribution for test statistics. **Multivariate statistical inference:** Techniques for drawing conclusions from data involving multiple correlated outcomes or parameters simultaneously. **Ordinal measures:** Statistics that assess association based on the rank order of the data rather than their numerical values. ## Multivariate Statistical Inference and Permutation Testing Publication Trend.
